title: The Impossible Triangle
description: Learn why no distributed system can guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once — and what real systems actually choose.

segments.text: Alright, this one is a big deal. The CAP theorem is probably the most cited — and most misunderstood — idea in distributed systems. Let's make sure you actually understand it.
Picture three database nodes. They all hold copies of the same data and they talk to each other over the network. Life is good. Reads and writes work perfectly.
In normal operation, when you write to node A, it replicates to B and C. When you read from any node, you get the latest data. Consistent and available. Everything you could want.
Now THIS is where it gets interesting. The network between nodes A and B breaks. They can't talk to each other anymore. This is a network partition — and it happens all the time in real systems.
Here's the million-dollar question. A write comes in to node A, but A can't reach B. What do you do? You have exactly two choices, and neither is perfect.
segments.thought_prompt: If node A can't replicate to node B, should it accept the write anyway or reject it?

segments.text: Choice one: refuse the write. Tell the client 'sorry, I can't guarantee consistency right now, so I'm going to block until the partition heals.' You keep consistency but sacrifice availability. That's CP — consistent and partition-tolerant.

Choice two: accept the write anyway. Node A stores it locally and will sync with B later when the network recovers. You stay available but now A and B have different data. That's AP — available and partition-tolerant.

And that's the CAP theorem in a nutshell. During a network partition, you must choose: consistency or availability. You cannot have both. Not because engineers aren't clever enough — it's mathematically proven.

So how do real systems choose? DynamoDB and Cassandra choose AP — they stay available and resolve conflicts later. Google Spanner and etcd choose CP — they block rather than serve stale data. Neither is wrong; it depends on your use case.
But here's something most people miss. Partitions are rare. What matters most of the time is the trade-off when there's NO partition.
segments.thought_prompt: When the network is fine, what trade-off do you still have to make between latency and consistency?

segments.text: That's where PACELC comes in. It says: if there's a Partition, choose A or C. Else, even in normal operation, you choose between Latency and Consistency. DynamoDB is PA/EL — it favors availability and low latency. Spanner is PC/EC — it favors consistency always.

So remember: CAP isn't about picking two out of three from a menu. It's about what your system does when the network breaks. And PACELC reminds you that the trade-offs exist even when things are working fine. That's the reality of distributed systems.
